correctness.rationale: A sufficiently small C2 perturbation of the unit-ball support satisfies the standard positive support-Hessian criterion and hence defines a smooth strictly convex body. Exact spherical moments show that its first support moment vanishes while the first moment of its squared support is nonzero. For a ball, optimization over all Euclidean isometries is exactly translation optimization; the p-power objective is coercive and strictly convex. The implicit-function theorem gives the unique optimal translation x_R=-C/R+O(R^-2), with C=6(p-2)(d-1)eps^2/((d+2)^2(d+4)) e1. Equivariance fixes the selector of a translated ball at its center, so association would force one target body to have a continuum of incompatible selector values. The packaged symbolic checker verifies every nontrivial algebraic coefficient.

originality.rationale: The 2009 Open Problem Session explicitly asks whether an isometry-equivariant selector associated with rho_p exists for p>2. The companion primary article defines rho_p and association, records the positive p=2 Steiner-point theorem, and proves nonexistence only for the Hausdorff metric. Later inspected selector and quotient-metric papers do not settle the finite-p>2 question. Exact-phrase, alias, support-function, and optimal-translation searches found no covering resolution.
residual_risks: A later unindexed note may have resolved Problem 13 without being surfaced by the searched terminology.
The proof covers finite p>2; the Hausdorff endpoint is prior and is not re-proved.
The general-dimensional convexity radius epsilon_d is existential rather than optimized.

value.rationale: The theorem gives a complete negative resolution of an explicitly published archive-era problem for every finite p>2 and every dimension d>=2. Its obstruction is structural: the unique nearest translation of a large ball moves by an explicit term proportional to (p-2)/R, explaining why the phenomenon begins exactly beyond the Hilbert exponent rather than producing only a single isolated counterexample.
